about: A PROJECT-DEFINED EDITORIAL EQUIVALENT, NOT AN EXTERNAL SYLLABUS. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO ANY ITALIAN EXAMINING BODY -- not to CILS (Universita per Stranieri di Siena) or CELI (Universita per Stranieri di Perugia), which core/exam-levels.json names as this track's exam, not to PLIDA, not to any university or ministry. AND NOTHING IN IT MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO DELE, THE INSTITUTO CERVANTES OR THE PLAN CURRICULAR ABOUT ITALIAN: they published a Spanish syllabus and have said nothing whatever about this language. READ THE THREE CLAIMS APART, BECAUSE THEY HAVE VERY DIFFERENT STRENGTHS. (1) THE POINT SET is derived structurally from core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, this project's restatement of the A1 grammar, function, notion and orthography inventories the Instituto Cervantes publishes behind DELE. That is the strongest thing here and all it establishes is a LEVEL: what an A1 candidate must be able to handle, asked as a language-neutral demand. (2) THE ITALIAN EXPONENTS are editorial throughout and are this project's judgement and nobody else's. THE PROXY SITS CLOSER HERE THAN ANYWHERE ELSE IN THIS SERIES AND THAT IS ITS OWN HAZARD. Italian and Spanish are sisters: two genders, pro-drop, a gustar/piacere frame built the same way backwards, an article system, written accents, the same alphabet. Nineteen previous tracks in this series had to restate every Spanish point around machinery the target language has instead; for Italian a great many points transfer almost unchanged, and the temptation is to let the Spanish sentence stand and call it Italian. Where the two diverge the divergence is recorded on the point itself and is usually the interesting part: the plural by vowel change rather than -s (IT-A1-N-06), the essere/avere auxiliary choice Spanish does not make (IT-A1-V-12), the accent that marks final stress rather than an exception to a stress rule (IT-A1-ORT-09), the article the possessive keeps (IT-A1-POS-03), the elision apostrophe Spanish has not got (IT-A1-ORT-11), and the doubled consonant that is real length (IT-A1-ORT-06). BECAUSE THE TWO LANGUAGES ARE SO CLOSE, NOT ONE PROXY POINT IS DROPPED: proxy.notTransferred is empty, and every one of the 273 Spanish points is answered by some Italian point. That is a claim about the language pair and not about the corpus, and it is the only inventory in this series that can make it. (3) THE COVERAGE NUMBER is a measure of the corpus against this list. It is not an exam-readiness claim and cannot become one while every scope dimension is partial. THE REGISTER COLUMN IS DERIVED FROM LESSON BODIES, NOT FROM FRONTMATTER, AND THE FRONTMATTER FIELD IS HALF-APPLIED RATHER THAN AN ARTEFACT: all 93 lessons declare variety: standard-contemporary, and register is non-neutral on exactly six of them while three further lessons teach the tu/Lei contrast in their bodies and declare neutral. IT-A1-REG-04 records that measurement. WHY A PROXY AT ALL: CILS and CELI are real published examinations and this project has not obtained a content inventory for either. NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION: no external search for one was performed for this file. code/learning/human-languages/BACKLOG.d records the sourcing question as settled and directs that it not be repeated per track (HL-C287, HL-C290). If somebody later reads a CILS A1 content list, this file should be rebuilt against it and the anchor kind changed from sourced-proxy to the real thing.
source: PROJECT-DEFINED. LEVEL PROXY: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, the DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Its own source is https://cvc.cervantes.es/ensenanza/biblioteca_ele/plan_curricular/niveles/02_gramatica_inventario_a1-a2.htm and the sibling function, notion and orthography inventories. Nothing about Italian is attributed to DELE, the Instituto Cervantes or the Plan Curricular. EXAM ENVELOPE: NONE EXISTS IN THIS REPOSITORY. Unlike latin/ and persian/, which ship assessment-spec.md, assessment.json and task-shapes/, the italian/ track ships no assessment spec, no assessment.json, no task shapes and no mocks, so no project-internal contract bounds the exponent choices or the gap notes below. This is separate from the EXTERNAL picture, where core/exam-levels.json records exam 'CILS / CELI', basis 'published', mapping 'identity' AND NO CAVEAT -- the only two tracks in this series so far with a published external exam and no caveat are italian and portuguese, and a published exam whose syllabus nobody here has read cannot bound anything either. PROFICIENCY BACKBONE: core/exam-levels.json, tracks.italian. CORPUS EVIDENCE: every probe was checked mechanically against the atoms declared by the 93 lesson files in code/learning/human-languages/italian/lessons/, which introduce 221 distinct atoms between them -- 81 ETYMON, 47 GRAMMAR, 41 LEX, 25 SOUND, 18 NOTICE, 6 PRAGMATIC, 2 PRAGMATICS and 1 PHONO. The last three kinds are the same kind under three spellings and the inventory probes all three. NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION: no external search for a CILS, CELI or PLIDA content syllabus was performed for this file. See `about`.

The only inventory in this repository that restates a real awarding body's published syllabus, so it is the only one that can lend a LEVEL. It lends a level and never a language, even to a sister language: nothing about Italian is attributable to DELE, the Instituto Cervantes or the Plan Curricular.

anchors.title: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume (2020), A1 descriptors
anchors.note: Public, third-party and language-neutral. It can anchor a FUNCTION -- can introduce himself/herself, can indicate when he/she is not following -- and it can never anchor an Italian form, because it names none. Used here only where a point is a can-do rather than a structure.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/italian/ -- 93 lessons across 25 chapters, curriculum.d and chapters.d
anchors.note: Our own work. It is what every probe resolves against and it is finite and auditable, but agreeing with it is not corroboration: the corpus cannot tell you what an exam would ask, only what this course happens to teach. Where a point's note says a word is missing, that absence was read out of this directory.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-levels.json, tracks.italian
anchors.note: Records Italian as exam 'CILS / CELI', basis 'published', mapping 'identity', with NO caveat. The absence of a caveat is why the register column of this file (IT-A1-REG-01 to IT-A1-REG-04) was measured from lesson bodies rather than imported from a sibling track's caveat.

anchors.title: This project's unaided judgement about Italian
anchors.note: Every Italian exponent below. Deciding that Spanish's three preterite points are answered by the single passato remoto, that the diacritic-tilde point is answered by e against e, that Spanish's superscript abbreviation letter transfers to Italy's raised ordinal indicator rather than dropping, and that a corpus with no negator cannot be credited with any function that needs one -- all of that is chosen here. It is a working default to be corrected, not a standard.

proxy.note: EMPTY ON PURPOSE, AND THIS IS THE ONE INVENTORY IN THE SERIES WHERE IT CAN BE. Every other track built on this proxy has had to drop Spanish points whose demand simply does not exist in the target language -- Tamil drops the written-accent rules because Tamil writes no accent, Bengali drops two. Italian is a sister language of the proxy: it has articles, two genders, adjective agreement, pro-drop, an inverted liking frame, written accents on the same alphabet and punctuation from the same tradition. Each of the 273 Spanish points was walked and each one names a real Italian demand, including the two that look Spanish-only: the general accentuation rules become Italy's final-stress accent (IT-A1-ORT-09), the diacritic tilde becomes e against e (IT-A1-ORT-10), the inverted question mark becomes the fact that Italian does not write one (IT-A1-ORT-13), and the superscript abbreviation letter becomes the raised ordinal indicator (IT-A1-ORT-16). RESTATING A POINT AROUND THE TARGET LANGUAGE'S MACHINERY IS DERIVING IT, NOT DROPPING IT, and an empty list here is that rule carried to its end rather than a walk that was not done.

communicative-functions.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's 54 A1 function points) and the Council of Europe CEFR Companion Volume A1 descriptors
communicative-functions.note: The proxy's functional column IS finite and level-split, which is what would close a dimension -- for Spanish. It does not close this one, because the exponent that realises each function in Italian is our choice every time, and a function inventory without its exponents is half a source. Italian ships no mock and no task shape to pin an exponent against, so no note here can say which paper item needs a word. One function is enumerated that the proxy has no A1 slot for and any beginner needs: saying that you have understood and that you have not (IT-A1-F2-17).

grammar.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's grammar, sentence and coordination columns)
grammar.note: THE DIMENSION THE PROXY HELPS MOST AND STILL DOES NOT CLOSE. Walking the Spanish grammar column surfaced demands no reading of the Italian corpus alone would have named -- that the plural article set is never stated, that the imperative is wholly absent, that non exists in the corpus only as part of a frozen phrase its own lesson defers. It does not close because a demand Spanish does not make can still be an A1 demand in Italian: the essere/avere auxiliary choice, the article a possessive keeps, the -isc- infix, the elision apostrophe. Those are enumerated on the project's judgement and, where the proxy has no slot at all, marked italianSpecific.

phonology-orthography.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json for the orthographic demands, and italian/pronunciation-reference.md
phonology-orthography.note: Italian and Spanish share an alphabet, so unlike the Indic and Arabic-script tracks in this series this column is not about a new writing system and the proxy's shape survives. What it cannot supply is the part of Italian spelling Spanish has no counterpart for: the doubled consonant as real length, the elision apostrophe, the ch/gh digraphs that keep a hard sound, and gli/gn/sc. The corpus is unusually strong on the sound side (the c/g softening rule is the most-repeated teaching point in the track) and empty on the punctuation side: not one punctuation mark is taught in 93 files. The pronunciation-and-prosody half of the source inventory is not level-split at all, which is the reason the proxy's own phonology dimension is partial, and that carries straight through to here.

lexicon.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's general and specific notion inventories)
lexicon.note: The proxy's notion inventories are what this column is walked against, at the granularity of their numbered subsections. They do not close it: which 500 Italian words an A1 candidate is expected to hold is exactly what an awarding body's word list would say and this project has not read one. What the column DOES do is name the shape of the corpus's lexical debt, and the shape is unusual -- the body, the family, the drinks, the days, the months and the numbers to twenty are all there, and the classroom, the shop, the journey, the house, the weather and every profession are all empty.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding -- an unmapped point is uncovered, never skipped, and its note is written as a work queue naming what would close it. Every atom named in every probe was checked mechanically against the 221 atoms the italian track actually introduces; a probe naming an atom that does not exist would report 'not covered' forever and be indistinguishable from real debt, so an id was never invented to fill a point, and no probe here points at a lesson somebody intends to write. ONE HABIT IS NAMED SO IT IS NOT A HIDDEN GENEROSITY: this track files most of its vocabulary under ETYMON rather than LEX -- 81 ETYMON atoms against 41 LEX -- because nearly every word lesson is built around where the word came from. giorno, sera, notte, ora, anno, pane, acqua, vino, the months and the seasons are all carried on an etymology atom. Probing those points therefore names an ETYMON id rather than a LEX one. The word IS introduced by that lesson; the track simply files it differently. A POINT IS NOT COUNTED AS COVERED WHEN ONLY PART OF WHAT IT NAMES IS TAUGHT, and that is where most of the uncovered points here come from rather than from total absence: si without no leaves polarity uncovered; domani without oggi and ieri leaves the time deictics uncovered; comprare without vendere leaves commerce uncovered; nine body parts with no verb of seeing leaves sight uncovered. That is deliberate, because a candidate asked for the other half of a pair gets no partial credit. `derivedFrom` records each point's provenance -- the proxy point ids whose demand it answers, or an empty list with `italianSpecific: true`. `anchorIds` records which anchor each point leans on, and the anchor's `kind` says whether that was something read or something decided. Neither field is read by any code; both are carried so the derivation can be audited rather than trusted.

points.label: proper nouns: a personal name, given and heard in an introduction
points.note: Chapter 3's exchange runs Marco and Giulia through a real introduction, and chapter 23 finally supplies nome itself, the word chapter 3 managed without.

points.label: place names: the city you live in and the city you work in
points.note: Roma and Milano are both used, in Abito a Roma and Lavoro a Milano. Two settlement names is more than most tracks in this series hold; see IT-A1-NE-73 for the word city, which is not taught.

points.label: common nouns naming periods of time
points.note: giorno, sera, notte, ora and anno. Filed as ETYMON atoms rather than LEX ones: this track carries most of its vocabulary on the etymology atom, and the note on probeSemantics says so.

points.label: gender: masculine in -o, feminine in -a, and learning a noun with its article
points.note: Chapter 1 states the rule and the habit together: two genders where Latin had three, and learn each noun with its article.

points.label: gender by heteronymy: the paired kinship words
points.note: padre/madre and fratello/sorella, chapter 10.

points.label: number: the plural made by changing the final vowel, not by adding -s
points.note: This is where the proxy earns its keep by being WRONG: the Spanish point is -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant, and the Italian demand behind it is a different mechanism entirely. Chapter 1 gives -o/-i and chapter 17 the three surviving declension classes.

points.label: nouns whose grammatical gender contradicts the world: la persona, la mano
points.note: Chapter 23 makes the general point (persona is feminine whoever it names) and chapter 17 the historical one (mano is feminine because manus was fourth-declension). A gender language could ask this of Spanish too; the PCIC A1 column does not, so it is enumerated here on our own judgement.

points.label: nouns that do not pluralise at all: il caffe, i caffe
points.note: Italian never pluralises a noun stressed on its own final syllable. Chapter 22 states it on the first such noun the track meets.

points.label: adjective agreement in gender and number
points.note: buono/buona/buoni/buone, and the buon giorno against buona sera contrast that makes the agreement audible on the first day.

points.label: the adjective used attributively, before its noun
points.note: buon giorno and buona sera are prenominal attributive adjectives, and the truncation to buon is taught with them.

points.label: the adjective used predicatively: il caffe e buono
points.note: The predicative frame, also with no new word: subject + essere + adjective. essere was chapter 16's and the four colours were chapter 13's, and no lesson had ever joined them, so il caffè è nero was unsayable although both halves had been on the page for a hundred lessons.

points.label: postnominal position, which is the Italian default
points.note: The Spanish point is postnominal-and-restrictive; Italian's ordinary attributive position is postnominal too (un vino rosso), and the only attributive adjective in the corpus is buon(a), one of the small class that goes in FRONT. So the learner has met exactly the exception and never the rule.

points.label: relational adjectives: the nationality and language word
points.note: italiano, in Parlo italiano. One gentilic, used as a language name; see IT-A1-NG-16 for using it to say where you are from, which the corpus does not reach.

points.label: degree: molto with an adjective, and the -issimo superlative
points.note: molto occurs three times in 93 files and every one is the fixed courtesy molto piacere. No lesson puts a degree word in front of an adjective, and -issimo is never mentioned.

points.label: the definite article: il, lo, la, and which noun takes which
points.note: Chapter 1 states the three-way split and chapter 22 lands it on zucchero, the first noun in the track that actually needs lo.

points.label: the elided article l' before a vowel
points.note: l'amico and l'amica, chapter 23.

points.label: the plural definite article: i, gli, le
points.note: i mesi and le stagioni are used as headwords in chapter 9 and i caffe in chapter 22, so the plural forms are on the page three times; no lesson ever states the set. A learner who has been taught to store every noun with its article has been given the singular half of that store only.

points.label: the indefinite article: un, uno, una
points.note: Taught as a side effect of the numeral: chapter 6's uno lesson says in as many words that uno is also a/an and flexes un/uno/una by the following sound.

points.label: the prepositional contractions: al, del, nel, sul
points.note: Italian contracts far more than Spanish, which contracts only al and del, so the demand behind the proxy point is LARGER here rather than smaller. The corpus never forms one. a Roma and a Milano are the only preposition-plus-place phrases and both take a bare noun.

points.label: the bare noun: where Italian uses no article at all
points.note: Parlo italiano is a bare noun and is taught as a whole sentence; ho venti anni is another. Neither lesson says that the article is absent or why.

points.label: the demonstrative forms: questo and quello
points.note: questo and quello, both. Neither word appeared anywhere in the track before this tranche; it was a whole column, not a gap in one.

points.label: spatial deixis, restated to Italian's two-way near/far
points.note: The two-way system, stated as two-way and contrasted with the Spanish three-way the proxy point describes, so a learner arriving from Spanish has one distinction to forget rather than one to learn.

points.label: position: prenominal, and incompatible with the article
points.note: Prenominal, and incompatible with the article -- questo caffè, never questo il caffè. No new word; and the point is worth its own lesson because it is the only place in the track where an article the reader was taught to store with every noun has to be taken back out. The possessive lesson three lessons later is the exact opposite rule and says so.

points.label: possessives for one possessor: mio, tuo, suo
points.note: mio, tuo, suo with all four endings, and the correction the old note asked for: the mi of mi chiamo is the reflexive myself, not a possessive. The lesson states the rule English speakers get wrong for years -- suo agrees with the thing owned and tells you nothing about the owner's sex.

points.label: possessives for several possessors: nostro, vostro
points.note: nostro and vostro -- and vostro was ALREADY IN THE READER'S MOUTH. The first lesson of the track traces ciao to the Venetian s-ciào vostro and glosses that vostro as `your`, and never names it as a word one could use. This lesson spends it. loro is given beside them as the invariable one, and credited to the essere table that already prints it.

points.label: the rule Spanish does not have: the Italian possessive keeps its article
points.note: The article the Italian possessive keeps, which is the whole of what this point is about, AND the kinship exception that takes it back -- mio fratello, i miei fratelli, il loro fratello, with all three conditions named. No new word: the article is chapter 1's, nome is chapter 23's, mio is two lessons back.

points.label: cardinal numerals 11 to 20, and the seam where the tens jump to the front
points.note: Chapter 12 does this properly: the six Latin fusions, then the reversal at diciassette, then where each Romance sister breaks.

points.label: cardinal numerals above 20
points.note: venti is the ceiling, and ho venti anni is the largest quantity a learner can state. Ages over twenty, prices, telephone numbers, years and room numbers are all out of reach behind this one gap.

points.label: ordinal numerals to tenth
points.note: CLOSED by the ordinal tranche. primo was the corpus's ONLY occurrence of an ordinal and it was inside a gloss -- primavera, 'the first green' -- so the tranche opens by giving the word behind that gloss. The order is Italian's own: primo and secondo carry no cardinal at all, terzo is the first in which one shows through, ottavo takes -avo and nono is a contraction, and each of those two gets a lesson. decimo closes the ten INHERITED words, and undicesimo then shows the seam -- above ten Italian drops the cardinal's final vowel and adds -esimo, which is one rule for the whole rest of the number line. NOT taught: the ordinal as a fraction beyond naming un terzo and un quarto, and the raised ordinal indicator, which is at IT-A1-ORT-16.

points.label: poco and molto, agreeing with what they quantify
points.note: molto and poco in both their jobs, with the rule that separates them: frozen before an adjective, agreeing before a noun. Before this tranche molto occurred three times in the track and every one was the fixed courtesy molto piacere; two of those three previews were removed from their lessons in the same commit, since this is the lesson that owns the word.

points.label: abbastanza
points.note: abbastanza, invariable, and the middle of a three-step scale the lesson lays out. It also gives Come stai? -- a question from chapter 2 -- its middle answer, abbastanza bene.

points.label: subject pronouns, singular: io, tu, lui/lei
subject pronouns, plural: noi, voi, loro
points.note: COVERED ALL ALONG, AND THE OLD NOTE WAS WRONG. It said the three plural pronouns are never named. They are: the essere lesson prints noi siamo / voi siete / loro sono and then tells the reader to KEEP loro where io sono and loro sono would collide, which is naming a pronoun and giving the condition for using it. andare, parlare and capire print the same set. This point was re-probed rather than authored against, and the tranche spent the lesson slot elsewhere.

points.label: pro-drop: why the subject pronoun is normally absent, and when it comes back
points.note: Chapter 3 states it and chapter 5 drills it, including the emphasis-and-contrast exception. Spanish is pro-drop too and the PCIC A1 grammar column does not enumerate it, so this is ours.

points.label: unstressed direct-object pronouns: lo, la, li, le
points.note: Absent. The learner has three verb classes and two past tenses and cannot say I took it.

points.label: the unstressed indirect object, in the piacere frame
points.note: Chapter 19 names mi as the one it pleases and makes il vino the subject.

points.label: the reflexive series: mi, ti, si
points.note: All three persons are given together in chapter 3, on chiamarsi, which is the verb an introduction actually uses.

points.label: the relative che with an overt antecedent
points.note: che, which returned exactly one case-insensitive match in the whole track before this tranche and it was the syllable CHE inside a pronunciation respelling. The lesson also collects a debt: chapter 3 taught twice that the h keeps c hard before e and i, once in piacere and once in mi chiamo, and che is the word that rule was for.

points.label: interrogative pronouns: chi, che cosa, quanto
points.note: chi, che cosa AND quanto. The first two are new; the third is unwelded rather than taught, because quanti was already in the track glued into the fixed age question Quanti anni hai? and the che cosa lesson takes it out and gives it its own meaning.

points.label: exclamative che with an adjective or adverb
points.note: Che buono! -- and this point is closed WITH NO NEW WORD. che is four lessons old by then and buono has been in the track since its first chapter, welded inside buongiorno, buonasera and buonanotte and never once said about anything.

points.label: stressed pronouns after a preposition: me, te, lui
points.note: me, te, lui, lei after a preposition -- the second pronoun set, which no preposition in the track had ever had after it. The lesson also gives A me piace against the mi piace of chapter 19 and says what the difference buys: Italian shouts a pronoun by swapping sets, not by raising the voice.

points.label: place deictics: qui and li
points.note: qui and lì, with qua and là named beside them. The etymology closes a thread three lessons long: ille gave the track its article in chapter 1, quello two lessons earlier, and now lì.

points.label: time deictics: oggi, ieri, domani
points.note: oggi and ieri, joined to the domani the track already had and had only ever used as the second half of the farewell a domani. The set now works with the two pasts the track teaches: Oggi lavoro a Roma, ieri ho lavorato a Milano.

points.label: quantity adverbs: poco, molto, abbastanza
points.note: All three quantity adverbs, which is what the point names.

points.label: manner adverbs: bene and male
points.note: Chapter 2 builds an answer ladder out of exactly these: (molto) bene, cosi cosi, non c'e male.

points.label: polarity: si and no
points.note: Both halves now, and the pair is taught as a pair. sì had been said out loud in chapter 5's dialogue since the track began and never given a line of its own; no was never an Italian word here at all. The no lesson also gives the split that makes the next point reachable: Latin nōn became a STRESSED no that stands alone and an UNSTRESSED non that leans on a verb.

points.label: connective adverbs: anche and neanche
points.note: anche and neanche, and neanche is taught as what it transparently is -- né + anche -- so the previous lesson has already paid for half of this one. anch'io / neanch'io is given as the pair, because between them they answer most of what anybody says to you.

points.label: interrogative adverbs: come and dove
points.note: come has a lesson of its own in chapter 2; dove arrives inside chapter 5's Dove abiti?.

points.label: perche: the one word that both asks and answers
points.note: perché, both jobs, in one lesson -- because that is what Italian does. The Spanish point spends itself on the por qué / porque split; the Italian demand behind it is that there is no split, and the lesson's worked exchange opens question and answer with the identical word.

points.label: present indicative: the regular -are class
points.note: Chapter 5 does this three times over and then drills it; it is the strongest single thing in the track.

points.label: present indicative: the -ire class and its -isc- infix
points.note: capire, with the infix given where the stress puts it and withheld from capiamo and capite.

points.label: present indicative: the plural persons of all three classes
points.note: -iamo/-ate/-ano in chapter 5 and again in its summary, and capiamo/capite in chapter 18. The endings are complete even though IT-A1-PRON-02 reports that the pronouns are not.

points.label: stare, and the essere/stare split
points.note: Chapter 2 sets identity against state, exactly as Spanish does, and gives the two forms the wellbeing exchange needs.

points.label: andare
points.note: Chapter 16 gives andare as a word built from two historical stems. Its present forms are not set out; the lesson's business is the suppletion.

points.label: the present's values: what happens now against what is going on
points.note: stare plus the gerund, which is how Italian says the second one, is never taught, and no lesson distinguishes parlo from sto parlando.

points.label: the imperfetto, for description and habit
points.note: Absent. Italian's everyday past for what things were like and what one used to do. The track reaches two other pasts and not this one, so a candidate can report a completed event and cannot describe a scene.

points.label: the passato prossimo with avere
points.note: Spanish's present perfect and Italian's passato prossimo are built the same way and used differently; the recipe is what this point asks for and chapter 15 gives it.

points.label: the passato prossimo with essere, and the participle agreeing with the subject
points.note: sono andato / sono andata, with the class of motion-and-change verbs named. Spanish has no auxiliary choice at all, so this demand is Italian's and is derived from the perfect point that is nearest to it.

points.label: irregular past participles: scritto, letto, preso
points.note: Chapters 18 and 19 hand over three that will not sit still, and chapter 20 then contrasts them with one that behaves.

points.label: stato: the participle essere borrows from stare
points.note: A whole lesson on one participle, because Latin esse never supplied one. Spanish solved the same problem by keeping ser and estar apart, which is why the proxy has no slot for this and the point derives from irregular participles instead.

points.label: the passato remoto
points.note: THREE PROXY POINTS LAND ON ONE. Spanish spends an A1 point each on the regular preterite, the strong stems and the ser/ir/ver/dar set; Italian's counterpart tense is one thing and chapter 15 reaches it. Read the coverage honestly: the lesson teaches parlo as a RECOGNITION target split by region, gives the third-person singular and no paradigm, so this point is covered at the level the lesson claims and not at the level a southern speaker would need.

points.label: the affirmative imperative, second person
points.note: No imperative anywhere in the corpus. prego (go ahead) is the only utterance in the track that does an imperative's work and it is a courtesy formula with no verb in it. Every instruction, request and direction in Italian is behind this point.

points.label: the infinitive, as the form a verb is stored and cited in
points.note: Every verb lesson is headed by its infinitive and every paradigm is cut from it by dropping -are, -ere or -ire.

points.label: the gerund
points.note: Absent, and it takes IT-A1-V-09 with it.

points.label: noun-phrase complements: an adjective, a di-phrase, a relative clause
points.note: None of the three is reachable: see IT-A1-ADJ-04 for the adjective, IT-A1-PRON-07 for the relative, and note that di appears in the corpus only inside piacere di conoscerti, quoted whole.

points.label: subject-verb agreement, stated as a rule
points.note: Chapter 8 makes it audible in a way a paradigm table cannot: e l'una against sono le due, where the verb changes because the number did.

points.label: the vocative
points.note: The vocative, and no new word is needed for it: Marco, buongiorno. Every practice exchange in the track opens with a bare greeting and never with a name, which is backwards, since it is the friend whose name you know. The lesson gives the two things Italian does not do here -- no article and no preposition.

points.label: piacere and its inverted argument structure
points.note: The frame the Spanish inventory spends its own point on, and Italian builds it identically. Chapter 19 says the wine does the pleasing.

points.label: the copula: essere for identity, stare for state
the attribute, and its agreement with the subject
points.note: The only subject agreement in the corpus is on the participle after essere. Adjectival attributes after a copula are not reachable; see IT-A1-ADJ-03.

points.label: the direct object
points.note: Ho preso il pane. The Spanish point is really about the personal a, which Italian does not write; the demand is restated as the plain transitive object and the corpus meets it once.

points.label: the indirect object, pronominal and prepositional
points.note: The mi of mi piace is an indirect object and chapter 19 describes what it does without naming it; the prepositional half (a Marco) never appears at all. Half a point is not a point.

points.label: circumstantial complements of place
points.note: Abito a Roma, e lavoro a Milano. The word-order flexibility the Spanish point also names is never stated, and Italian's is narrower than Spanish's anyway.

points.label: the affirmative declarative
points.note: Parlo italiano is announced by its own lesson as the learner's first self-assembled sentence.

points.label: the negative declarative, with non
points.note: THE TRACK'S MOST CONSEQUENTIAL GAP, CLOSED, AND IT WAS ONE WORD. non goes immediately before the verb and Italian needs no helper the way English needs `do`. The lesson works the rule on five sentences the track had already taught and could only say one way round, and it pays the debt the non c'è male lesson booked in chapter 2 by name.

points.label: yes-or-no questions, by intonation alone
points.note: Parli italiano?. Italian, like Spanish, inverts nothing and adds no particle, so intonation is the whole mechanism and the dialogue models it.

points.label: questions with an asking word
points.note: Come stai?, Dove abiti?, Quanti anni hai?. Three asking words in three chapters.

points.label: impersonal existence: c'e and ci sono
points.note: c'è and ci sono, and the lesson is where non c'è male finally comes apart. The chapter 2 lesson that taught that phrase said in as many words that its negation and its c'è belonged to later lessons; this tranche pays both, four lessons apart, and the second one quotes the deferral.

points.label: copulative and attributive sentences
points.note: Marco e italiano, given in chapter 16 as the worked example of the written accent.

points.label: transitive and intransitive sentences
points.note: Italian carries the distinction where a learner can hear it -- in the auxiliary -- and chapter 16 states the motion-and-change class that takes essere. Spanish's own transitivity point has no such handle.

points.label: copulative coordination with e
points.note: THE ONLY JOINING WORD IN THE TRACK, and it arrives sideways. Chapter 16's lesson on the written accent has to gloss plain e as and in order to contrast it with e; chapter 5's dialogue then uses it for real, in Abito a Roma, e lavoro a Milano. Counted as covered on that basis, and the reader should know how thin the basis is: no lesson is about coordination, and E tu? / E Lei? are learned as whole turn-handing formulas.

points.label: negative coordination with ne
points.note: né … né, with the doubled negative stated as the requirement it is: Non prendo né caffè né tè carries three negatives and Italian wants all three. Ordered after non deliberately, because né cannot stand without it.

points.label: disjunctive coordination with o
points.note: o. Every raw match for it in the track before this tranche was a letter named in a pronunciation note or a vowel in an etymology.

points.label: adversative coordination with ma
points.note: ma, whose only previous match in the track was inside the Latin de mane behind domani. Its etymology spends a word the reader owns: Latin had two words for MORE, and Italian kept plūs as the più of a più tardi and turned magis into but.

points.label: distributive coordination: uno ... l'altro
points.note: Absent.

points.label: infinitive clause as subject
points.note: Absent. The infinitive is taught as the citation form only.

points.label: infinitive clause as direct object: voglio parlare
points.note: Absent, and the modal verbs that would take one (volere, potere, dovere) are absent too.

points.label: finite clause as direct object, with penso che
points.note: penso che. pensare had a lesson of its own in chapter 18 and nothing was ever put after it; che, one lesson earlier, is the thing that goes after it. The lesson names the congiuntivo, says spoken Italian uses the plain present constantly, and does not teach it.

points.label: restrictive relative clause with an expressed antecedent
points.note: Restrictive relative with an expressed antecedent: l'amico che parla italiano.

points.label: che as relative subject and as relative object
points.note: Subject and object both, and the lesson makes the point that Italian does not ask you to tell them apart -- che is the same word in l'amico che parla and il caffè che prendo, where English picks who against that and may drop the word entirely.

points.label: causal clauses with perche
points.note: Causal clauses. The track had spent its whole length explaining why Italian words are shaped as they are and had no way to let a learner say because.

points.label: purpose clauses with per plus an infinitive
points.note: per + infinitive, and NO NEW WORD: per arrived one lesson earlier inside perché, and every infinitive in the examples was taught between chapters 5 and 20. What is new is the infinitive doing a job -- it had been the track's citation form since chapter 5 and had never appeared inside a sentence.

points.label: simultaneity with quando
points.note: quando, which returned zero occurrences before this tranche. Taught in both its jobs, and the etymology is the rarest kind in this track: quandō changed almost not at all in two thousand years, which the lesson contrasts with the five reshaped words the reader already holds.

points.label: ask for information about a person, a thing or a place
points.note: Come ti chiami? and Dove abiti?. Both are person questions; nothing in the corpus asks about a thing.

points.label: give personal information: name, age, where you live
points.note: All three are reachable, which is unusual in this series; the age answer is capped at twenty by IT-A1-Q-03.

points.label: ask for confirmation with a tag question
points.note: vero? and no? both, which is what this point asked for. The vero lesson gives the one shape that answers every English tag -- isn't it, doesn't he, aren't you -- and says which answer it expects.

points.label: confirm or deny the previous statement
points.note: Confirming and denying, both. The denial half was the one the whole track lacked.

points.label: ask for an opinion by handing the turn back
points.note: E Lei? in the formal exchange and E tu? in the informal one. Learned whole, and they are what an A1 conversation actually uses.

points.label: give an opinion with penso che
points.note: Giving an opinion, with the frame the proxy point names.

points.label: ask for an evaluation
points.note: Come va? asks how a thing is going, which is the evaluation question this level wants.

points.label: evaluate with bene, male and a middle term
express approval and disapproval
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express agreement
points.note: d'accordo, plus anche/anch'io. Anch'io had been in chapter 5's dialogue unglossed since the track began and is now named; d'accordo is new, and its etymology spends the cuore the body chapter already taught -- ad + cor, cordis, bringing two hearts together.

points.label: express disagreement
points.note: Non sono d'accordo. Both halves are new in this tranche and the negation lesson works this sentence explicitly, because until it the track could agree and had no way to disagree with anything.

points.label: show scepticism with non so
points.note: Non so, and the lesson treats the slow hanging Non so … as the politest disagreement in the language. No new word: non is two chapters old and so is one lesson old.

points.label: offer a counter-argument with ma
points.note: Offering a counter-argument. The lesson also gives the bare sentence-initial Ma …, which is nearer English `well …` than `but`.

points.label: express certainty by plain assertion
points.note: The cheapest point in the inventory, and worth enumerating anyway: a plain declarative IS the A1 way of being certain, and the track can build one.

points.label: express possibility
points.note: forse and potere are both absent.

points.label: ask whether somebody knows something
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express knowledge, with sapere or conoscere
points.note: SAPERE WAS THE ONLY MISSING HALF, AND THE OLD NOTE WAS WRONG ABOUT THE OTHER. It said neither verb is taught and that conoscere is on the page once inside a fixed courtesy. In fact the incontrare lesson teaches conoscere as incontrare's partner -- incontrare is the event, conoscere the acquaintance -- gives its etymology from cognōscere, and puts it in the past. Only sapere was absent, and the sapere lesson is where the two are finally set against each other.

points.label: express ignorance of something
points.note: Ignorance, including the hedge that puts a question word after it -- Non so quando, Non so perché, Non so chi è. Those question words are the joining chapters', and non so is what lets a learner use them about themselves rather than only to ask.

points.label: ask about ability to do something
points.note: Parli italiano?, which is the exact A1 exchange this point exists for.

points.label: express ability, and hedge it
points.note: Si, parlo un po'. The hedge un po' is unglossed (IT-A1-Q-05) but the whole answer is drilled twice in the same lesson, so the move is available even though its parts are not.

points.label: say that you have understood, and that you have not
points.note: THE REPAIR COLUMN, CLOSED. capire and capisco were taught in chapter 18 and non arrived one lesson before this one, so the lesson invents nothing; what it adds is the ORDER -- Non capisco. Prego? -- and the reason for it, which is that Prego? alone gets the same sentence at the same speed.

points.label: ask about a preference by offering alternatives
points.note: Asking about a preference by offering alternatives -- Caffè o tè? Both nouns were already taught; only the single letter between them was missing. NOT the same as expressing one: IT-A1-F3-03 (preferisco) stays uncovered and is named there.

points.label: express a preference with preferisco
points.note: A near miss worth naming for the author who fixes it: preferire is an -isc- verb and chapter 18 teaches that whole pattern on capire, so the machinery is in place and only the word is missing.

points.label: express wishes with volere or vorrei
points.note: Absent. This is the single word that unlocks ordering, asking and inviting at this level.

points.label: ask about plans and intentions
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express plans and intentions
points.note: andare is taught as a word in chapter 16 and never as the auxiliary of intention, and the corpus has no future of any kind -- not the periphrasis, not the futuro semplice.

points.label: give an order or an instruction
points.note: See IT-A1-V-17: there is no imperative in the corpus.

points.label: ask for an object, softened
points.note: per favore returns ZERO occurrences in 93 files. The track teaches four separate uses of prego and never teaches please. A learner can thank, answer thanks, hand something over and stand aside, and cannot ask for anything.

points.label: ask for help
points.note: Chapter 19 teaches aiutare and, with it, the one-word shout an Italian street uses.

points.label: respond to an order, request or plea
points.note: prego, go ahead.

points.label: grant permission
points.note: The same exponent doing the same work at a doorway; chapter 2 gives it its own lesson.

points.label: refuse permission
points.note: Unreachable: refusing needs no or a negated verb.

points.label: offer an object
points.note: prego while handing something over, chapter 2.

points.label: invite somebody to do something
points.note: Absent, and behind both the imperative and volere.

points.label: accept a proposal, offer or invitation
points.note: Sì, grazie -- and the lesson names the trap: Italian uses grazie for BOTH accepting and declining, where English swaps please for thank you, so a bare grazie at an Italian table is heard as a refusal.

points.label: decline a proposal, offer or invitation
points.note: No, grazie. Same lesson as IT-A1-F4-09; enumerated apart because a candidate who can only accept is not at parity with one who can also decline.

points.label: greet by the time of day
points.note: buongiorno, buonasera and buonanotte, all in chapter 1, and each assembled from parts the learner already has.

points.label: respond to a greeting
points.note: Chapter 2's exchange models the whole return turn, including Bene, grazie.

points.label: address somebody by name or title
points.note: signore, signora and signorina, with il signor Rossi and the reason for the missing -e. The track taught the formal Lei and the come sta / come stai contrast and had nothing to put after either. dottore, ingegnere and the rest of the Italian title habit are still absent.

points.label: introduce a third person
points.note: Questo è Marco. Chapter 3 taught the whole of introducing YOURSELF and left the third person out, because a third-person introduction needs a pointing word and the track had none.

points.label: respond to an introduction
points.note: piacere, with the nod and the handshake described.

points.label: apologise
points.note: scusa, scusi and mi dispiace return ZERO occurrences between them in 93 files. Alongside the missing please, this is the second courtesy move a beginner needs on day one and does not have.

points.label: thank, and answer thanks
points.note: Both halves, in chapter 1 and chapter 2.

points.label: offer condolences
points.note: Absent.

points.label: propose a toast
points.note: cin cin and salute are both absent, although chapter 11 teaches vino.

points.label: congratulate
points.note: Absent.

points.label: take leave naming when you will meet again
points.note: a domani, a presto, a piu tardi -- a whole chapter on choosing the promise that fits.

points.category: Funzioni: gestire la conversazione (discourse and repair)
points.label: open a conversation

points.category: Funzioni: gestire la conversazione (discourse and repair)
points.label: greet and respond within a conversation

points.category: Funzioni: gestire la conversazione (discourse and repair)
points.label: ask for a person, on the telephone or at a door
points.note: pronto is absent, and so is every telephone word; see IT-A1-NE-36.

points.category: Funzioni: gestire la conversazione (discourse and repair)
points.label: show that one is following what is said
points.note: No backchannel of any kind: not si, not certo, not capisco used as a listening token.

points.category: Funzioni: gestire la conversazione (discourse and repair)
points.label: REPAIR: signal that you did not hear, and ask for it again
points.note: THE REPAIR COLUMN, THE OTHER HALF, AND THE TRACK HAS ONE. Chapter 2 gives rising Prego? a lesson of its own and states what separates it from flat prego: the intonation and the situation. That is a genuine repair move, taught deliberately, which several tracks in this series do not have at all. What is still missing: non ho capito, puo ripetere, piu lentamente, come si dice -- all of them behind the negator, the imperative or the modal.

points.category: Funzioni: gestire la conversazione (discourse and repair)
points.label: ask somebody to be quiet
points.note: Absent; behind the imperative.

points.category: Funzioni: gestire la conversazione (discourse and repair)
points.label: propose closing the conversation
points.note: E stato un piacere. Arrivederci! -- chapter 4 supplies the pre-closing as well as the closing.

points.label: possession and having, with avere
points.note: Chapter 14 is built on it: ho venti anni, hanno venti anni, and the silent h that keeps hanno apart from anno.

points.label: presence and absence: con and senza
points.note: Neither preposition occurs. c'e is unreachable (IT-A1-OS-05).

points.label: general quality, with essere
points.note: Marco e italiano is the corpus's one predication of a quality, and the quality is a nationality.

points.label: locating an event in time
points.note: The clock lesson tells the time and never dates an event; the weekday, month and season lessons name the units and never put anything in one. La festa e domenica is unsayable.

points.label: certainty and uncertainty
points.note: Absent; see IT-A1-F2-11 and IT-A1-F2-14.

points.label: numerical quantity
points.note: One to twenty, and no further; the ordinals the Spanish point also names are reported separately at IT-A1-Q-04.

points.label: relative quantity: piu, meno, molto, poco
points.note: piu occurs only inside the farewell a piu tardi, where it is glossed as part of the phrase and never as a comparative.

points.label: degree: molto, un po'
points.note: Degree, molto and un po' -- and un po' is UNWELDED rather than taught. Chapter 5's dialogue said Sì, parlo un po' and never glossed it; this lesson says what it is (poco with its last syllable cut off, marked by an apostrophe and not an accent) and why a speaker reaches for it rather than poco.

points.label: measures: size, distance and weight
points.note: Absent.

points.label: location: saying where you are
points.note: Abito a Roma and Lavoro a Milano put a person in a place. Location is carried by the verb of living and working, not by a locative adverb, because IT-A1-ADV-01 reports none.

points.label: relative position: vicino, lontano, destra, sinistra
points.note: Absent.

points.label: distance
points.note: Absent.

points.label: movement and stability
points.note: andare, and the essere-taking class of motion verbs -- venire, arrivare, partire -- named as a class in chapter 16.

points.label: orientation and direction
points.note: Absent.

points.label: order: ordinals, prima and dopo
points.note: CLOSED. prima and dopo each get a lesson, and the recombining lesson works both systems on the same four things -- the courses of a meal -- so the difference between naming a place (il primo) and naming a relation (dopo il primo) is worked rather than stated. prima is taught as what it is: the feminine of primo, frozen from Latin prima 'at the first', which is why Italian's word for before IS its word for first. The ordinals are at IT-A1-Q-04. NOT taught: poi and infine beyond one occurrence each in the recombining lesson.

points.label: origin: essere di plus a place, and the nationality word
points.note: italiano is taught as a LANGUAGE name inside parlo italiano and never as an origin, and sono di ... never appears. A learner who can say which two cities they live and work in cannot say where they are from.

points.label: the clock, and the parts of the day
points.note: Chapter 8 gives the hour with its feminine article and the agreement that goes with it, plus noon and midnight; chapter 1 gives the parts of the day inside the greetings.

points.label: locating in time: weekdays, months, seasons
points.note: Complete: seven days, twelve months, four seasons, chapters 7 and 9. The today/yesterday/tomorrow half of the Spanish point is reported separately at IT-A1-ADV-02 and is not covered.

points.label: anteriority and posteriority
points.note: CLOSED with IT-A1-NG-15 and by the same two words, both taught in the temporal sense as well as the sequential one: prima di cena, dopo cena, prima o poi, dopodomani. The two past tenses this track teaches are still never set in order against each other, which was the second half of the old note; that needs a tense lesson, not a vocabulary one.

points.label: sight
points.note: occhio is taught as a body part in chapter 24 and vedere is not taught at all. The organ without the verb.

points.label: hearing
points.note: orecchio is taught in chapter 24; sentire and ascoltare are absent. The same shape as IT-A1-NG-20.

points.label: colour
points.note: Five colour words in chapter 13, with the Latin, Germanic and Arabic roads they came in by. Nothing is ever described as being one of them; see IT-A1-ADJ-03.

points.label: open and closed, way in and way out
points.note: Absent.

points.label: general evaluation: bene, male, cosi cosi
points.note: The chapter 2 answer ladder, which is a genuine three-term scale rather than the single positive word most tracks in this series manage.

points.label: value and price
points.note: quanto costa is absent, and every number above twenty is absent with it (IT-A1-Q-03), so the answer would be unsayable even if the question were taught. Two gaps, one hole.

points.label: attractiveness: bello, brutto
points.note: Absent.

points.label: quality: essere buono, essere cattivo
points.note: buono is taught only as the first half of a greeting and never predicated of anything; cattivo never appears.

points.label: acceptability
points.note: Absent.

points.label: conformity: d'accordo
points.note: Conformity, in the word Italians actually use for it.

points.label: correctness: right and wrong
points.note: bene and male are taught as answers about how one is, never as verdicts on whether something is right. giusto and sbagliato are absent.

points.label: interest
points.note: interessante is absent. mi piace expresses liking and is counted at IT-A1-F3-01; it is not the same notion and is not double-counted here.

points.label: capacity and competence, with sapere
points.note: sapere plus an infinitive, which is how Italian says CAN in the learnt-how sense. The ability question the track already reached (Parli italiano?) uses the plain present of the activity verb; so parlare says what parlo cannot, that you learnt it.

points.label: ease and difficulty
points.note: Absent.

points.label: reflection and knowing: the verbs of mind
points.note: Chapter 18 IS this notion: pensare to weigh, capire to seize, leggere to gather, scrivere to scratch, four minds' worth of Latin and every one of them physical first.

points.label: parts of the body
points.note: NINE body words across chapters 17, 24 and 25 -- the densest specific-notion block in the track and more than the proxy point asks for.

points.label: physical characteristics
points.note: alto, basso, giovane, vecchio: none of them. Nine body parts and no way to describe a body.

points.label: actions and positions of the body
points.note: stare is glossed etymologically as to stand and is taught as the verb of state, never as a posture.

points.label: character and personality
points.note: Absent.

points.label: personal data: the name and the age
personal data: surname, address, telephone number
points.note: cognome, indirizzo and numero di telefono are all absent, which is most of what an A1 form asks for.

points.label: documents: passport and identity card
points.note: Absent.

points.label: personal objects
points.note: Absent.

points.label: family relationships
points.note: padre, madre, fratello, sorella and famiglia itself.

points.label: social relationships: the friend
points.note: amico and amica, taught as a gendered pair, which also carries IT-A1-ART-02's elision.

points.label: social relationships: colleague, boss, neighbour
points.note: Absent.

points.label: celebrations and family, social and religious occasions
points.note: Absent.

points.label: drink
points.note: acqua, vino, caffe, latte, te -- five, and chapter 22 is built around them.

points.label: foodstuffs
points.note: pane and zucchero. Two, which is thin, and they are the two an A1 breakfast needs.

points.label: the meals of the day
points.note: colazione, pranzo and cena are absent. The track has the parts of the day and not the meals named after them, which is an odd near-miss given that chapter 1 teaches giorno, sera and notte.

points.label: dishes and courses
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the bar and the restaurant
points.note: prendere is taught in chapter 19 WITH its table sense (at a table, to have), which is precisely the verb an Italian bar order uses. There is nothing to order with it, nobody to order from, no word for bar or ristorante, no please and no numbers over twenty for the price. The verb is the only piece present.

points.label: educational institutions
points.note: Absent.

points.label: teaching staff and students
points.note: Absent.

points.label: timetable, examinations and marks
points.note: Absent.

points.label: learning and teaching
points.note: imparare and insegnare are absent; capire and leggere are the nearest and belong to the mind rather than the classroom.

points.label: classroom language
points.note: One utterance in the whole corpus would survive a classroom: the rising Prego? of IT-A1-F6-05. Come si dice, non ho capito, puo ripetere and the rest are absent.

points.label: teaching materials and classroom furniture
points.note: Absent.

points.label: working activity
points.note: lavorare, with the city it is done in. The verb is present and every noun around it is not.

points.label: professions and posts
points.note: Absent. A learner can say that they work and never what they do, which is the most common A1 introduction question after the name.

points.label: workplaces, tools and work clothing
points.note: Absent.

points.label: unemployment and job-seeking
points.note: Absent.

points.label: rights and obligations at work
points.note: Absent.

points.label: what a worker is like
points.note: Absent; behind IT-A1-NE-04 as well.

points.label: games and playing
points.note: giocare and suonare, split as Italian splits them and English does not.

points.label: free time and entertainment
points.note: Absent.

points.label: shows and exhibitions
points.note: Absent.

points.label: sport
points.note: The etymology of portare names English sport in passing and no sport is taught. giocare is present, so the verb an A1 sport sentence needs is there and every sport is not.

points.label: information and communication media
points.note: Absent.

points.label: written correspondence
points.note: scrivere is taught in chapter 18 and nothing is written to anybody: no lettera, no email, no caro/cara, no saluti.

points.label: the telephone
points.note: Absent, pronto included; see IT-A1-F6-03.

points.label: the printed press
points.note: Absent.

points.label: television and radio
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the internet, and dictating an e-mail address
points.note: Absent, and doubly out of reach: dictating an address needs the letter names, which IT-A1-ORT-01 also reports missing.

points.label: living somewhere
points.note: abitare, chapter 5. Buying, selling and renting a dwelling are not reachable; comprare is taught (chapter 20) and has nothing to buy.

points.label: types and parts of a dwelling
points.note: casa is absent, which is striking beside abitare.

points.label: domestic activities
points.note: Absent.

points.label: household objects and furniture
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the postal service
points.note: Absent.

points.label: financial services
points.note: Absent.

points.label: health services
points.note: Absent.

points.label: protection and security services
points.note: Aiuto! is taught as the shout an Italian street uses, which is how one summons them, and no service is named.

points.label: shopping: buying
points.note: comprare, chapter 20. The place, the person and the thing are all missing; see IT-A1-NE-59.

points.label: clothing, footwear and accessories
points.note: portare is taught WITH its wear sense in chapter 20 and there is not one garment in the corpus to put after it.

points.label: payment
points.note: Absent; see IT-A1-NG-26.

points.label: health and illness
points.note: The wellbeing exchange of chapter 2 is about mood, not health, and its own lesson treats it that way. malato, star male and mi fa male are absent -- and gola and stomaco ARE taught, which is exactly where an A1 complaint would land. The nearest miss in the whole inventory.

points.label: centres of health care
points.note: Absent.

points.label: medicine and medicines
points.note: Absent.

points.label: hygiene
points.note: Absent.

points.label: travel objects and documents
points.note: Absent.

points.label: accommodation
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the transport system
points.note: Absent. andare is taught and there is nothing to go in and nowhere named to go except Roma and Milano.

points.label: finance and money
points.note: Absent.

points.label: commerce: the buyer and the seller
points.note: comprare is taught and vendere is not, so the transaction has exactly one side.

points.label: businesses and organisations
points.note: Absent.

points.label: industry and energy
points.note: Absent.

points.label: mathematics: the notion of number
points.note: Chapter 12 does more than list numerals: it takes the fusions apart and shows the ten inside them.

points.label: computing and new technology
points.note: Absent.

points.label: political institutions and government
points.note: Absent.

points.label: law and justice
points.note: Absent.

points.label: music: playing an instrument
points.note: suonare, taught beside giocare in chapter 21 precisely so the learner does not merge them. The verb is there and not one instrument is.

points.label: artistic disciplines
points.note: Absent.

points.label: architecture, sculpture and painting
points.note: Absent.

points.label: literature and reading
points.note: leggere is taught in chapter 18 and no book, poem, writer or newspaper is named.

points.label: photography
points.note: Absent.

points.label: cinema and theatre
points.note: Absent.

points.label: religion
points.note: The corpus touches religion only in etymology -- pregare behind prego, sabato as the Sabbath, domenica as the Lord's day -- and teaches no religious word as a word.

points.label: geography: country, town, city, capital
points.note: Roma and Milano are used as NAMES (IT-A1-N-02) and citta, paese and capitale are all absent, so a learner can name two Italian cities and cannot say the word city, or the name of the country whose language they are learning.

points.label: the universe and space
points.note: Chapter 7 walks the planet-gods behind lunedi to venerdi, and names them as LATIN sources for the day words; luna, sole and stella are never taught as Italian words.

points.label: urban and rural spaces
points.note: Absent.

points.label: climate and weather
points.note: Absent, which also removes the commonest A1 small-talk opener there is.

points.label: fauna
points.note: The gloss of italiano as perhaps calf-land is the only animal in 93 files.

points.label: flora
points.note: primavera is glossed as the first green and no plant is named.

points.label: the alphabet, and the names of the letters
points.note: The track never says the alphabet aloud. It teaches a great deal about how letters SOUND and never what they are CALLED, which is what spelling a surname or dictating an address needs.

points.label: the vowel letters, and the open and closed vowels behind them
points.note: Taught as named sound tags -- vowel-a-open, open-o -- rather than as an inventory. Italian has seven vowel sounds behind five letters, which is a demand Spanish's five-for-five system does not make.

points.label: the consonant letters: c and g, hard and soft
points.note: The single most-repeated teaching point in the track: c and g soften before e and i and stay hard elsewhere, stated on come, piacere, prego and leggere.

points.label: the digraphs ch and gh, which keep c and g hard
points.note: Italian ch is a hard k, the opposite of English, and chapter 21 shows the h being INSERTED to save the sound when giochi takes its ending.

points.label: the digraphs gli, gn and sc
points.note: gn is mentioned once, in the list of clusters that take lo, and never taught as a sound; gli appears only in the plural article, which IT-A1-ART-03 reports untaught; sc never appears. Three of Italian's most distinctive spellings, none of them read.

points.label: the doubled consonant, which is real length
points.note: double-tt on quattro and sette, double-zz on mezzo, and anno held audibly in chapter 14. Spanish has no length contrast, so this whole demand sits behind a spelling point the proxy states for a different reason.

points.label: s and z: when a single letter is voiced
points.note: Chapter 25 states the rule (a single s between vowels is voiced) and chapters 1 and 18 give the z and the exception after n.

points.label: capital letters, and where Italian keeps lower case
points.note: Italian writes languages, nationalities, weekdays and months in lower case, as Spanish does and English does not. The corpus writes them correctly on every page and never states the rule, so a learner has seen italiano and lunedi a hundred times and has not been told why.

points.label: the written accent that marks a final stressed vowel
points.note: Italy's accent rule is not Spain's, and this is where the proxy is most usefully wrong: Spanish accents mark an exception to a stress rule, Italian's mark a stressed final vowel and almost nothing else. cosi, lunedi, caffe, piu -- four instances, each taught where it falls.

points.label: the accent that separates two spellings: e against e
points.note: The exact counterpart of Spanish's diacritic tilde, and Italian's most-used instance. si/si, la/la and da/da are the rest of the family and none of them is taught.

points.label: the apostrophe of elision
points.note: l'amico, l'una, un po'. Spanish has no elision apostrophe at all, so the demand is Italian's; it is derived from the spelling point rather than invented because the proxy's column is where a writing-system rule belongs.

points.label: the full stop and the comma
points.note: No punctuation mark is taught anywhere in the track. Every mark on every page is used correctly and none is named.

points.label: question and exclamation marks -- and the opening pair Italian does NOT write
points.note: Restated rather than dropped: the Spanish point is about the inverted opening marks, and the Italian demand behind it is knowing that they are Spanish and that Italian writes only the closing one. Neither the marks nor the contrast is taught.

points.label: the colon, parentheses, quotation marks and the dash in dialogue
points.note: The practice dialogues are set with the em-dash speaker mark throughout, which is the Italian convention and is never mentioned.

points.label: the hyphen and the slash
points.note: Absent.

points.label: abbreviations, initialisms, symbols, and the superscript ordinal indicator
points.note: STILL UNCOVERED, and now for a narrower reason than before. The ordinals themselves are taught (IT-A1-Q-04) and the numeral-plus-raised-letter form is the only piece of this group an ordinal tranche could reach; it is deliberately NOT claimed here, because the raised indicator needs U+00BA and U+00AA added to core/main-font-charset.json and this tranche did not touch that file. Sig. and Dott. are also still absent. THE SPANISH SUPERSCRIPT POINT STILL TRANSFERS RATHER THAN DROPPING. The fix names itself: one charset addition plus one lesson.

points.label: the tu/Lei choice, made as a grammatical choice
points.note: Chapter 2 does this properly and early: Lei is literally she, often capitalised, and takes the third-person verb, so Come sta? and Come stai? differ by grammar and not by tone.

points.label: choosing the greeting by register
points.note: ciao against buongiorno, with buongiorno explicitly named the safe respectful choice for shopkeepers, strangers and elders.

points.label: switching register inside one exchange
points.note: Chapter 2's practice runs the SAME exchange twice, formal and informal, and chapter 3 does it again for names. Running one dialogue at two registers is what an examiner would actually test and the track does it twice.

points.label: what the frontmatter register field records, against what the lessons teach
points.note: MEASURED, NOT IMPORTED, because core/exam-levels.json carries NO caveat for italian. All 93 lessons declare variety: standard-contemporary, so that field carries no information. register is declared non-neutral on exactly SIX lessons -- ciao and its writing lesson (informal), come-sta (formal) and the three prego lessons (polite) -- and it MISSES the register teaching it should catch: come-stai, come-ti-chiami and buongiorno all declare neutral while their bodies teach the informal/formal contrast in as many words. So the field is not an artefact the way a uniformly-neutral track's would be, and it is not a usable index either: the three points above were read out of lesson BODIES, and this fourth point records that the field would have found only half of them.
